titre: The Twelve Tables, the Roman law that was never found again
accroche: Around 450-449 BCE, Rome set its law in writing for the first time. Not a fragment has survived: we know it only through quotations by later authors.
contenu_vulgarise:
In front of the Curia, in the Roman Forum, twelve tablets are fixed to the Rostra. Livy says they are bronze, Pomponius says ivory: the sources do not agree on this point. What matters is that any Roman can now stop in front of them and read, with his own eyes, the rules that govern him. Before 449 BCE, this law was still largely customary: unwritten, it was interpreted by the pontiffs, priests drawn from the elite, and administered by the patricians, first of all in their own interest.

## A concession won by walking out

Since the founding of the Republic in 509 BCE, only patricians can hold a magistracy. The plebeians, who make up Rome's labor force, have a formidable weapon: secession, a mass departure from the city that brings the Roman economy to a halt. By this means they obtain, according to the tradition reported by Wikipedia, the codification of a law that had until then remained largely customary. A first board of ten men, the decemvirs, drafts ten tablets in 451 BCE. Livy tells that an embassy was sent to Greece to study the constitution of Solon in Athens; modern historians doubt this and think rather of contact with the Greek cities of southern Italy. A second decemvirate adds two tablets in 450, then a new plebeian secession forces the Senate to examine the last two; the whole is ratified by the centuriate assembly in 449 BCE.

## What the text says, and what it does not change

The translation from the Avalon Project (Yale Law School) gives an idea of the content. Table VIII distinguishes the thief caught at night, whom the owner may lawfully kill on the spot, from the unarmed thief caught by day, who is whipped and then handed over as a bondsman to his victim. Table V keeps women under guardianship even as adults, because of their "levity of mind," with the exception of the Vestal Virgins. Table X limits funeral expenses, down to the number of mourners and flute players allowed. These rules can now be read by all, but they are no more favorable to the plebeians for that: the same law forbids them, in Table XI, to marry a patrician. Writing the law down did not make it fairer. It only stopped being interpreted by a single order.

The real shift lies elsewhere. The Twelve Tables themselves have not survived: not a fragment, original or copied, has come down to us. According to Paul R. Coleman-Norton's edition, they were probably destroyed when the Gauls took Rome in 387 BCE. Everything we know of them comes from quotations by later authors. Cicero, in his treatise *De Legibus* (On the Laws, II, 23, 59), recounts that the schoolboys of his childhood still learned the Twelve Tables by heart, "ut carmen necessarium," like a song one had to know. The first Roman law written so that everyone could read it without an intermediary is therefore known only through quotations and testimonies from later authors: the engraved text is gone, but Cicero attests that it was still being recited in his day.

carte.punch: Around 449 BCE, Rome set down its first written law. Not a single fragment of it has ever been found.
carte.idee: The Twelve Tables, Roman law's first written code, around 450-449 BCE, no longer exist. We know them through quotations by later authors, including Cicero, who recounts that in his childhood schoolboys learned them by heart like a required song.

quiz.question: Why do the plebeians obtain, around 450-449 BCE, that Roman law be put in writing?
choix: So that the law would stop being in the hands of the pontiffs and patricians
To obtain the abolition of the distinction between patricians and plebeians
To replace the Roman magistracies with a single court
So that Rome would directly adopt the laws of Solon, enacted in Athens
quiz.explication: Before the Twelve Tables, Roman law remained largely customary, interpreted by the pontiffs and administered by the patricians, first of all in their own interest. Writing does not abolish the patrician-plebeian distinction, still present in Table XI, does not touch any magistracy, and does not directly take over the laws of Solon: the embassy to Greece reported by Livy is itself doubted.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What remains today of the original text of the Twelve Tables?
choix: Not a fragment, original or copied: the text is known only through quotations by later authors
The first ten tablets, engraved in bronze, kept in the Roman Forum
A complete copy found in the archives of the Capitoline
Only Table XI, on the ban on marriage between the orders, has been found
quiz_supplementaire.explication: No fragment of the Twelve Tables, original or copied, has survived: they were probably destroyed when the Gauls took Rome in 387 BCE. Everything we know of them comes from quotations by later authors, including Cicero.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Cicero (De Legibus, II, 23, 59), how did the schoolboys of his childhood learn the Twelve Tables?
choix: By heart, like a song one had to know ("ut carmen necessarium")
By copying each tablet by hand onto a wax tablet
By attending their public recitation at the Forum every year
They did not learn them: only future pontiffs studied them
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Cicero recounts that, in his childhood, schoolboys had to learn the Twelve Tables by heart, "ut carmen necessarium," like a required song. Nothing in the sources mentions individual handwritten copying, an annual public recitation, or study reserved for future pontiffs.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the tradition reported by Livy, what did the decemvirs do before drafting the Twelve Tables?
choix: Send an embassy to Greece to study the constitution of Solon
Consult the patrician pontiffs, who would have drafted the text in their place
Convene an assembly of plebeians to dictate the law themselves
Take over unchanged the customary law already applied by the courts
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Livy reports that an embassy was sent to Greece to study the constitution of Solon in Athens, an account modern historians doubt, thinking rather of contact with the Greek cities of southern Italy. Nothing indicates that the drafting was entrusted to the pontiffs or to the plebeians themselves, or that the existing customary law was simply taken over.
